tagline: Granite spires and a stage-road canyon link Albion with Oakley.
intro: The City of Rocks Backcountry Byway crosses the Albion Mountains through rural country punctuated by granite spires. Its paved approach becomes a narrow, winding road between Connor Creek and Almo, then gravel from Almo to Oakley. Visit Idaho includes this backcountry route among the state’s scenic byways and emphasizes its geology and rural landscape. The tourism office gives the 49.4-mile drive a travel time of one hour and 18 minutes. Along Birch Creek, the landscape closes into a narrow canyon with high volcanic cliffs, between Middle Mountain on the west and the Albion range on the east.

In the 1840s and 1850s, California Trail wagon trains left the Raft River valley and crossed City of Rocks on their way over Granite Pass into Nevada. After the transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869, regional wagon and stage routes continued serving places beyond the rails. The Kelton-to-Boise stage route passed through City of Rocks; the modern byway follows its corridor along Birch Creek.

Begin in Albion on Idaho 77, continue to Connor Creek Junction, then travel through Elba and Almo to City of Rocks National Reserve. Beyond the reserve, the route turns north along Birch Creek toward Oakley and its junction with Idaho 27.

moments.title: Almo
moments.text: Almo is a ranching community below 10,399-foot Cache Peak, just over two miles east of City of Rocks National Reserve. The town developed around a post office established in 1881 on land that had been part of Myron B. Durfee’s ranch. By the turn of the century, Almo had a school, a brass band and a theatrical group as well as a store and post office. The reserve’s headquarters is in Almo. The visitor center for both the reserve and Castle Rocks State Park is at the south end of town, linking this ranching settlement with the two protected landscapes.

moments.title: City of Rocks National Reserve
moments.text: Axle grease became a writing material at City of Rocks. California-bound emigrants left names and initials on Register Rock, where those marks remain visible alongside a landscape bearing wagon-wheel ruts. During the 1840s and 1850s, wagon trains crossed this granite country from the Raft River valley toward Granite Pass and Nevada. The area became a national reserve in 1988 for its historical and geological values, scenery and recreation. The granite rises from rolling sagebrush country. Erosion along fractures has shed thin plates and scales from the rocks, shaping the formations that frame the emigrant route.
moments.notice: Names and initials written in axle grease remain visible on Register Rock.

moments.title: Oakley
moments.text: Oakley’s historic district includes Victorian houses and the Howells Opera House. The theater, completed in 1907, was built from local quartzite known as Oakley stone. Its square gable false front has a central doorway flanked by segmental-arched openings. Nearby quarries produce Oakley Stone for use as a building material. Within the town’s historic district, stone and brick buildings stand alongside its Victorian houses. When demolition was discussed in the 1970s, local performers formed the Oakley Valley Arts Council and bought the building. The council continues to stage seasonal performances there.
